# Your tool: two tracks, one course

The principles are the course. The tool is your choice, and **the free one is the classroom.** On the free track you can finish the whole course without buying anything.

## Free track: Grease Pencil, in Blender (the classroom)

Blender is free and open source. Grease Pencil is its 2D animation toolset: frame-by-frame drawing, onion skinning, layers, a camera, and sound on the timeline. Studios use it in real productions. Joshua Leung started it in 2008; who built it since is told below.

**Before Module 1:**

1. Install **Blender 5.2 LTS**.
2. Open it and start a **new file from the 2D Animation template**.
3. Find where the **frame rate** is set, and set it to **24 frames per second**.

→ [download Blender](asset:blender_download) · [manual: Grease Pencil, the quick start](asset:gp_intro) · [manual: where to set the frame rate](asset:blender_format)

**Every assignment works in either tool.** The steps show Blender, and "what good looks like" is always about the motion. The paid track, Toon Boom Harmony, is optional and described below.

{{deeper}}

## The free Kick-Start course

Whatever track you are on, Toon Boom's **Harmony Essentials Kick-Start** course is free with a free account: three modules, about 2 h 40 min in total. The course points you to the right part each week.

→ [the Kick-Start course](asset:harmony_kickstart)

## Paid track, optional: Toon Boom Harmony (the industry field trip)

Harmony is widely used in TV animation. It costs money, with a student rate you can check for yourself. It also has a **14-day free trial**, which this course places in **Module 7**, so the trial covers the two weeks you make your final piece.

→ [Toon Boom's shop, for current prices and the student rate](asset:toonboom_shop)

## Drawing input

A drawing tablet or a mouse both work. The input changes your technique, not whether you can take the course.

## Where the tool came from

Grease Pencil started in 2008 as a simple note-taking feature by Joshua Leung. A small team later rebuilt it for 2D animators: the developers Antonio Vázquez and Clément Foucault, and the artists Daniel M. Lara and Matías Mendiola. Their short film *Hero* was paid for by the people who used the software.
